title: VB4-02597
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (the "applicant") has applied to the Immigration and Refugee Board to find that the refugee protection of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "respondent") has ceased, pursuant to s.108(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1
The Applicant alleges that the Respondent's situation is described in s.108(1)(a) of the Act, i.e. a person who has "voluntarily reavailed themself of the protection of their country of nationality."

To summarize the background of this application: the Respondent, a citizen of Honduras, came to Canada in September 2014 and made a refugee claim against Honduras that was accepted by a member of the Refugee Protection Division on March 21, 2005.
On XXXX XXXX, 2006, the Respondent became a permanent resident of Canada.
The Respondent applied for and received a Honduran passport, valid from XXXX, 2009 to XXXX, 2014.
He used this passport to travel back to Honduras five times between 2007 and 2014.

On August 28, 2014, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Canada provided their Application for Cessation of Refugee Protection, consisting of a notice, grounds for the application, and a volume of supporting documentation, including material obtained via CBSA interviews with the Respondent.

On November 29, 2017, the Refugee Protection Division provided a notice to the parties that they should appear for a hearing on this matter on February 16, 2018. This matter was subsequently rescheduled.
On June 11, 2018, the Respondent disclosed documents for the hearing.
On June 22, 2018, the parties appeared at a hearing in Vancouver, BC. A second hearing day was then scheduled.
On July 16, 2018, the Respondent provided written submissions requesting that the application be rejected for reasons of procedural fairness.
On August 3, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions on the procedural fairness argument.
On October 3, 2018, the second hearing day took place, which completed the evidentiary portion of this matter.
On October 17, 2018, the Applicant provided written submissions regarding the evidence and analysis of re-availment.
On October 29, 2018, the Respondent provided written submissions on the evidence and analysis of re-availment.
On November 9, 2018, the Applicant provided reply submissions. Applicant's Position
The Applicant's position is summarized from their submissions.

The Applicant notes that, per the UNHCR Handbook, there are three criteria for re-availment. The refugee must have: * Acted voluntarily; * Intended by his action to re-avail himself of the protection of the country of nationality; and * Actually obtained such protection.
Regarding voluntariness, the Applicant notes that there is no evidence that the Respondent was instructed to obtain a Honduran passport.

Regarding intention, the Applicant submits that the Respondent's two applications for Honduran passports and presentation of his documents to government officials (or agents) while travelling indicate that he intended to avail himself of the diplomatic protection of Honduras. The Applicant additionally submits that, while in Honduras, the Respondent was not "clandestine or cloaked in secrecy in any reasonable way."

Regarding actual obtention of protection, the Applicant notes that the Respondent did receive two passports and was allowed multiple entries to a number of countries, which amounts to receipt of diplomatic protection.
For these reasons, the Applicant argues that the conditions of re-availment under s.108(1)(a) have been met. Respondent's position
The Respondent's position is summarized from their submissions.
The Respondent seeks to have the application dismissed. The Respondent advances two arguments.
First, the Respondent submits that the issue of re-availment arose from an abuse of process.
The Respondent notes that, while returning to Canada through Vancouver International Airport on XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Respondent was examined by a CBSA Officer.
The Respondent acknowledges that the CBSA Officer had a duty to determine whether the Respondent was a valid permanent resident for the purpose of allowing him to enter Canada per s.19(2) of the Act.
The CBSA Officer went on to ask additional questions, regarding the Respondent's refugee status, returns to Honduras, and his fears.

The Respondent argues that the CBSA Officer ought to have informed the Respondent that he was under no obligation to answer these additional questions, and that he had a right to counsel being present, before examining him on matters which go beyond his statutory authority.

The CBSA Officer's examination led to a follow-up interview of the Respondent by a CBSA Hearings Advisor, who collected more information and took a copy of the Respondent's passport. The Hearings Advisor did tell the Respondent that he was under no obligation to answer the questions, but failed to advise him of a right to counsel.

The Respondent notes that s.167 of the Act confers a right to counsel at "proceedings before any Division of the Board and the Minister," and that, per the Federal Court of Appeal,2 such proceedings include pre-hearing evidence-gathering interviews.

The Respondent argues that the Panel has the authority and obligation to exclude the evidence adduced in violation of natural justice. Excluding the improperly obtained statements and documents collected by the CBSA Officer and Hearings Advisor would leave the Applicant without an evidentiary foundation for its application.
The second argument of the Respondent is that the Applicant failed to meet its onus to establish that the Respondent voluntarily re-availed himself of the protection of Honduras.
The Respondent does not dispute the Applicant's accounting of his travel dates and locations, or the use of Honduran documents.
The Respondent submits that the primary issue before the Panel is to assess the motivation to obtain a passport and return to Honduras.
The Respondent notes that he was effectively isolated from his family because of his protection status in Canada. This isolation placed him in a difficult position.
According to his credible testimony, the Respondent took a calculated risk in obtaining Honduran documents for the purpose of seeing his son and to attend to his aging parents who were in ill health.

Accordingly, the Respondent submits, he did not return to Honduras of his own free will, but was "compelled by his love, affection, and circumstances." His intent to request a passport was not, in that sense, truly voluntary.
Regarding protection, the Respondent submits that a distinction must be made between contacting authorities to obtain protection, and contacting authorities for any other purpose.

The Respondent argues that "acquiring a passport is not a determining but a neutral factor in this Application," in that the Respondent never filed a refugee claim on the basis of a fear of the authorities. Rather, the Respondent feared, and continues to fear, non-state agents of persecution.

The Respondent did not seek the protection of the authorities in his returns to Honduras. He kept a low profile during his returns, staying at home and other safe areas, avoiding friends and neighbours, and using agents to assist with obtaining documentation. His subjective fear persisted.
The application of the Applicant is rejected. Analysis
I find that the Applicant provided ample notice to the Respondent of its application and supporting facts.
I also find that both parties had sufficient opportunity to argue their respective points, at the hearing and through written submissions.

As stated to the parties during the hearing, the analysis commences with the Respondent's procedural fairness argument that unfairly obtained material should be deleted, leaving no evidentiary basis for a finding of cessation.

The Respondent's objections are clearly argued and supported by case law which confirms that evidence-gathering interviews are "hearings" that require the person considered to be notified of a right to counsel.

I acknowledge the Applicant's argument that the case cited by the Respondent was determined after the airport interview in 2014. However, a retroactivity/retrospectivity argument does not invalidate the need to conduct official interactions in a way that conforms to the law as it is understood today.
Based on the evidence and law before this Panel, the right to counsel for hearings exists, and that right was not made clear to the Respondent when obtaining his information.

I find that the case law and natural justice considerations oblige the Panel to disregard material obtained as a result of non-jurisdictional interviews done without the benefit of notice of right of counsel.

This is the approach taken by the RPD in a different cessation application, VB4-01404.3 This decision is not binding on other RPD Panels, but I adopt its reasoning with respect to the exclusion of evidence.
For these reasons, I have not considered the questions and answers from the CBSA Officer4 and Hearings Advisor.5

Evidence that has not been excluded because of fairness reasons include the Respondent's Declaration Card stating that his citizenship is "Residents,"6 and his permanent resident card, passport, and boarding pass.7
I find that the above materials would reasonably have been provided by the Respondent in order to show who he is, and that he is a person eligible to return to Canada.

To the argument of the Respondent that this leaves the Applicant with nothing upon which to advance its cessation request, the Applicant replies that returning to Canada on a Honduran passport after receiving Convention Refugee status is sufficient to make a prima facie case for cessation of his status.
I agree that the Applicant's case would have been clear, and perhaps strong, with these stated documents in hand, plus the knowledge that the Respondent had been a refugee claimant.

The crucial question then arises: how did the Applicant come to know that the Respondent was a Convention Refugee, apart from the improperly-obtained admission that he is a former refugee claimant who has no fear of Honduras?
I do not see a clear answer in the evidence.

One could speculate. It's quite possible that refugee determination is a status that is available via database to CBSA officers who work at points of entry, and that such information is automatically flagged, or that there is a policy to routinely seek immigration history when determining eligibility to enter Canada.

To go even further, I suggest it is entirely reasonable for CBSA officers to make these checks when examining people for eligibility to enter. Refugee status being a highly limited exception to the immigration procedures of signatory nations, Canada has every right to gather information for cessation and vacation applications in order to remove those who do not need protection.
However, the evidence does not tell me that the CBSA officer, prior to improperly questioning the Respondent, actually spotted his refugee determination on the computer system.

I do not believe that such a consequential matter as cessation of a person's refugee status should hinge on things that are technically possible, and out of simple common sense ought to have been done. Where there is insufficient admissible evidence, the Panel cannot approve the application.

In this case, I find that the Applicant has not provided sufficient admissible evidence that the CBSA Officer knew, at the airport, that the returnee was a past recipient of refugee protection, thereby justifying further investigation and ultimately this application for cessation.

On the evidence, and for the foregoing reasons, I find that the Applicant has not met its onus to show that the Respondent, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a person who has voluntarily re-availed himself of the protection of his country of nationality.

The application is therefore dismissed.
